root.claim: One deterministic fixed-alphabet, fixed-tape Turing machine multiplies two $n$-bit integers in $O(n(\lg n)^{1-\kappa})$ worst-case time, where $\kappa=2^{-182}$.
root.method: Reduce the product to a convolution of radix digits evaluated by synthetic-transform Fourier transforms, and cut the cost of their data movement and arithmetic with two power-saving tape procedures built on finite linear networks

motivation.text: Scanning $\Theta(n)$ bits at each of $\Theta(\log n)$ transform levels already costs $\Theta(n\log n)$, so both movement and arithmetic must be sped up.

quote.quote: We therefore need savings in both movement and arithmetic.

children.claim: The scaled and rounded output coefficients equal the exact integer coefficients of the radix-digit product, and carry propagation yields the exact $2n$-bit product.
children.method: Remove the known normalizations, bound the accumulated error below $1/2$ so that rounding is exact, then propagate radix-$2^b$ carries

motivation.text: The approximate transforms only give coefficients up to a small error, and the true coefficients are integers, so exactness follows once the error is below one half.

children.claim: The final absolute error of each coefficient is less than $448b\,2^{-b+\gamma}\le 448b\,2^{-3b/4}<1/2$, so the nearest integer is the correct coefficient.
Radix-$2^b$ carries, defined by $d_j=(c_j+k_j)\bmod 2^b$ and $k_{j+1}=\lfloor (c_j+k_j)/2^b\rfloor$, stay below $2^{2b}$ and give the exact $2n$-bit product.

children.salient: The error bound $448b\,2^{-3b/4}$ is below $1/2$ only because $p=6b$ leaves $b$ bits of room after the normalizations, and $\gamma=o(b)$; the page should explain why these powers of two compensate.

children.claim: Every normalized cost, divided by $Tp$, is at most $p^{1-2\kappa}$, so the total cost is $O(n(\lg n)^{1-\kappa})$ with $\kappa=2^{-182}$.
children.method: Tabulate the normalized cost of each operation as a power of $p$, take the smallest margin below one, and absorb any fixed power of $\log p$

motivation.text: Each operation has cost $Tp$ times a power of $p$; the total is governed by the largest power, so only the margins to $1$ matter.

children.claim: The smallest margin below one among the seven dominant powers is $\min_i g_i=2^{-181}=2\kappa$.
Hence the total cost is $O(Tp\,p^{1-\kappa})=O(n(\log n)^{1-\kappa})$, and with schoolbook multiplication below a cutoff the machine has worst-case time $O(n(\lg n)^{1-\kappa})$.

children.salient: The smallest margin is $g_2=\epsilon c(1-\tau)=2^{-181}$, a tiny quantity coming from the chunk-exchange row; the page should explain why the exponent $\kappa=2^{-182}$ is half of this margin and how it comes from the chosen constants $\epsilon=2^{-75}$, $c=2^{-56}$ and $1-\tau=2^{-50}$.

root.salient: The saving is a power of the logarithm, $(\lg n)^{-\kappa}$, with an astronomically small but positive exponent, so $n\log n$ is not a lower bound. The page should explain why the saving is a power rather than a smaller factor, from the strict inequality $s<Wm$ shared by both tape procedures.
